hook.text: A small shop's checkout works. Then the business asks for a second shipping rule, a text message beside the confirmation email, and a count for the loyalty program.

hook-ask.text: Each request is small. Whether it lands as a new piece, or as an edit to code that already works, depends on how the objects were drawn.

plan.text: Fifteen questions on object-oriented design, argued on that one shop. Eight get a figure each, and seven go quickly at the end.

coh.text: Question one. What are cohesion and coupling? Cohesion is how focused a class is: its methods and data all serve one clear purpose. Coupling is how much modules depend on each other. Low coupling means a change in one rarely forces a change in another.

coh-god.text: Here's the anti-pattern. One order manager prices the cart, charges the card, writes the invoice, sends the email and updates the stock. It's a god class, a pocketknife with a blade for everything.

coh-cost.text: That's five reasons to change in one class, and everything that touches an order depends on all five. A new email template means retesting checkout.

coh-split.text: Split it into five focused pieces, each with one job and a narrow connection to the rest: high cohesion, low coupling. Most of SOLID pushes this way.
coh-split.spoken: Split it into five focused pieces, each with one job and a narrow connection to the rest: high cohesion, low coupling. Most of solid pushes this way.

coh-spot.text: To spot one in a review, count a class's reasons to change, and count what has to change with it.

comp.text: Question two. Why favor composition over inheritance? Inheritance ties a subclass to its parent's implementation, so a change upstream can break it. That's the fragile base class problem.

comp-cart.text: The shop's loyalty program extends the shopping cart, and counts each item as it's added. The cart's add-all adds them one at a time, so three items count three.

comp-break.text: Then the cart team speeds add-all up, and it stops adding them one at a time. The count for those three drops to zero, and nobody touched the loyalty code.

comp-hold.text: Composition holds a cart and delegates to it, counting in its own methods. It relies only on what the cart promises: three before the change, three after.

comp-mix.text: It also combines freely. Notifications go by email, text or push, at one of three timings. A subclass per pair is nine, and a fourth channel makes twelve. Composition gives each notifier one channel and one timing: six parts, then seven. A customer who switches to the daily digest swaps one part, at runtime.

comp-when.text: Keep inheritance for a genuine subtype. Which raises what makes one genuine.

lsp.text: Question three. What is the Liskov substitution principle, in plain terms? A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without surprising the caller.

lsp-square.text: The classic trap is a square that subclasses a rectangle. It keeps its sides equal, so setting its width sets its height too.

lsp-break.text: Code written for rectangles sets the width to five, then the height to four, and expects an area of twenty. Hand it a square, and it gets sixteen.

lsp-rule.text: So a subclass mustn't demand more of its callers, or promise them less.

lsp-fix.text: And the fix isn't a cleverer square. Don't make a square a kind of resizable rectangle: shapes that can't be resized, or two siblings that each work out their own area, both keep every promise.

solid.text: Question four. Walk through the SOLID principles. Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change. The invoice changes only when its layout does.
solid.spoken: Question four. Walk through the solid principles. Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change. The invoice changes only when its layout does.

solid-o.text: Open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification. A new shipping option arrives as new code, not as an edit to what works.

solid-l.text: Liskov substitution: subtypes stand in for their base type, which the square couldn't.

solid-i.text: Interface segregation: many small interfaces over one fat one. The stock screen only reads stock, so it shouldn't depend on an interface that also issues refunds.

solid-d.text: And dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, and inject the concrete pieces. That's the next question.

solid-laws.text: They're guidelines for low coupling and high cohesion, not laws. Applied everywhere, they produce the over-engineering this video ends on.

dip.text: Question five. What is the dependency inversion principle, with an example? High-level code depends on an abstraction, and the concrete implementation is passed in.

dip-ex.text: The order confirmation needs something that can send a message, and that's all it knows. In production, it's handed the email sender. A test hands it a fake that only records what it was asked to send, and checks the message with no mail server.

dip-plug.text: It's a lamp with a plug, instead of wires run into the wall. The socket is the abstraction, and anything that fits it works.

dip-arrows.text: The inversion is in the arrows. The confirmation no longer points at the emailer; the emailer fits the shape the confirmation asked for. Policy stops depending on detail.

strat.text: Question six. What is the Strategy pattern? It puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, and lets the caller pick one at runtime, instead of a sprawling if-else.

strat-ship.text: A shipment holds a pricing strategy and asks it for the cost. For a parcel weighing three, the flat rate says five. Pricing by weight, at two a unit, says six.

strat-third.text: A third rule, free above a weight of ten, is a new class. The shipment isn't edited: that's open-closed.

strat-one.text: With only one rule, though, the interface is just indirection. A plain function does the job until a second rule really arrives.

obs.text: Question seven. What is the Observer pattern? A one-to-many dependency: when a subject changes state, it notifies every observer that registered.

obs-order.text: An order is placed. The email, the stock count and the analytics have each subscribed, and each one hears about it. The order doesn't know their types, so a fourth, for loyalty points, joins without an edit to the order.

obs-use.text: It underpins event systems, UI data binding, and publish-subscribe.

obs-cost.text: The cost is indirection. Reading the checkout no longer tells you what happens after an order; you have to go and find who subscribed.

over.text: Question eight. When does a design pattern become over-engineering? When it adds indirection without a need to match.

over-ex.text: A factory for a class that will only ever have one implementation. A strategy interface with one strategy. An observer with one hard-coded listener. Each is abstraction you have to read through, for flexibility nobody uses.

over-yagni.text: Patterns solve variation you expect. Added speculatively, they break YAGNI: you aren't gonna need it.
over-yagni.spoken: Patterns solve variation you expect. Added speculatively, they break yag-nee: you aren't gonna need it.

over-trigger.text: So in an interview, name the trigger rather than the pattern. The second shipping rule is the day the strategy earns its interface. Reach for a pattern when the duplication, or the pressure to change, is real.

rapid-in.text: Seven more, a sentence or two each.

r-pillars.text: The four pillars of OOP. Encapsulation bundles data with its methods and hides the state. Inheritance reuses and specializes a class. Polymorphism gives one call the right behavior for each type. Abstraction shows what an object does, not how.

r-encap.text: Encapsulation, concretely: an account hides its balance and changes it only through methods that check, so no withdrawal can overdraw it. Guard every way in, the constructor too. An account that opens at minus fifty is overdrawn already.

r-poly.text: Polymorphism, by example: total area asks each shape for its own area, a circle and a square alike, with no ladder of type checks.

r-factory.text: A factory centralizes creation, so callers ask for what they want, like a parser for CSV, not how to build it. It pays off when the class depends on runtime input, or construction is complex.

r-single.text: A singleton is one instance with a global access point, like a config. It's controversial as global mutable state: it hides dependencies, and a test that passes alone can fail after one that changed the config. A module-level value or plain injection is often cleaner.

r-abstract.text: An interface declares what methods a type must provide, with no implementation. An abstract class can also share code and state. Use an interface for a pure contract, and an abstract class when subclasses share code.

r-isa.text: And is-a versus has-a. A car is a vehicle: inheritance. A car has an engine: composition. Make car extend engine, and it inherits the engine's whole interface. Ask which it is before you inherit.

next.text: Every answer here assumed you were the one writing the code.

next-read.text: Most of the code you'll be asked about, you didn't write. Next: reading and reviewing code.
